tagline: Switchbacks climb from Sonoran cactus country to fir and aspen.
intro: The Catalina Highway climbs through switchbacks from Tucson’s desert floor toward Mount Lemmon, gaining more than 6,000 feet. It is the Sky Island Scenic Byway, a National Scenic Byway that the Federal Highway Administration presents as a journey from saguaro cactus to conifer forest. The Forest Service compares its 27 miles of changing vegetation to traveling from Mexico’s deserts to Canada’s forests. Overlook turnouts provide places to stop along the climb. Along the ascent, saguaro, mesquite and cholla give way to oak, juniper and pinyon, followed by pine forest and fir and aspen on cooler north-facing slopes.

Former postmaster general Frank Harris Hitchcock organized support for an improved road to Summerhaven and nearby mountain facilities. Construction began in 1933 and, the Forest Service records, ended in 1950. A federal prison camp supplied much of the labor. The highway took Hitchcock’s name after his death in 1935. A series of road improvements begun in 1988 widened the highway and added shoulders, passing areas and guardrails; the last project finished in 2007.

From Tanque Verde Road in northeast Tucson, enter Coronado National Forest and climb through Molino Canyon. The road passes Willow Canyon, the Rose Canyon Lake turnoff and Soldier Camp before reaching Summerhaven. The final section turns east toward Ski Valley and ends near Mount Lemmon’s summit.

moments.title: Gordon Hirabayashi Recreation Area
moments.text: The highway’s construction camp held Japanese American prisoners during World War II, including draft resisters and Gordon Hirabayashi, who challenged exclusion from the West Coast. Prisoners drilled dynamite holes, broke rock with sledgehammers and cleared trees for the Catalina Highway. The camp had no security fence. White-painted stones marked its boundaries, and its expanded facilities included barracks, a mess hall and staff cottages. The site became a youth rehabilitation center in 1967; it closed in 1973, and the buildings were destroyed afterward. Foundations and walls remain at the site, which was named for Hirabayashi in 1999.
moments.notice: Foundations and walls survive from the camp’s demolished buildings.

moments.title: Summerhaven
moments.text: Summerhaven is a mountain community surrounded by pines, with both seasonal and year-round residents. The Aspen wildfire struck in summer 2003 and destroyed more than 250 of the community’s 700 homes. In the months afterward, Tucson residents organized “Lemmon Aid” to help rebuild. Most of the village’s small cabins were rebuilt after the fire. The settlement sits approximately 7,600 to 8,200 feet above sea level, reached from northeast Tucson by the Catalina Highway. The highway journey from the mountain’s base to the community is about 24.5 miles, placing the village near the upper end of the ascent.

moments.title: Mount Lemmon
moments.text: Mount Lemmon is the highest mountain in the Santa Catalina range, within Coronado National Forest north of Tucson. An Air Force radar base once occupied the site of Mount Lemmon’s summit observatory. The military facilities passed to the Forest Service, and the University of Arizona leases the observatory’s land and buildings. Telescopes here serve astronomical research and teaching programs, including the Catalina Sky Survey and Astronomy Camp. The mountain’s name honors botanist Sara Plummer Lemmon, who reached the top with her husband and rancher E. O. Stratton by horse and on foot in 1881.
